sentences.text: The anterior section of the lower jaw featured a flattened surface ending in a downward-pointing extension.
Dental elements were laterally compressed and equipped with serrated edges for processing food.
This predator possessed a robust neck coupled with a relatively small shoulder girdle structure.
It ranks among the most massive theropod dinosaurs, although fragmented fossils complicate precise size calculations.
Measurements for the primary specimen indicate a total length of 12 to 13 meters, a skull measuring 1.53 to 1.80 meters, and a femur of 1.365 to 1.43 meters.
In 1993, an amateur hunter named Rubén Darío Carolini found a leg bone while driving near Villa El Chocón in Neuquén province, Argentina.
The main type specimen was later unearthed in the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia during the same year.
Scientists Coria and Salgado formally described the species Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995.
The specific name carolinii was chosen to honor the discoverer, Ruben Carolini.
Evidence suggests this animal maintained a constant body temperature with a metabolic rate intermediate between mammals and reptiles, allowing for rapid development.
It could snap its jaws shut rapidly to seize prey and inflict powerful crushing forces.
Researchers propose that the chin structure helped the skull withstand stress generated during high-impact biting.
Fossilized footprints attributed to this genus show three toes with large, rough digits and distinct claw marks.
Additional anatomical traits placed this dinosaur outside the advanced group known as Coelurosauria.
By 1996, Sereno and associates classified Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Acrocanthosaurus within the superfamily Allosauroidea and the family Carcharodontosauridae.
In 2004, Thomas R. Holtz and team defined the family Carcharodontosauridae as allosauroids more closely related to Carcharodontosaurus than to Allosaurus or Sinraptor.
Later, in 2008, Sereno and Stephen L. Brusatte united Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, and Tyrannotitan into the tribe Giganotosaurini.
This creature inhabited the region now known as Patagonia, Argentina, between 99 and 95 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage.
Studies by Sereno and others indicate that carcharodontosaurids were distributed across continents by the Early Cretaceous period.
Scientists argue over whether Giganotosaurus exceeded the size of Tyrannosaurus, matched it, or if its maximum estimates are overstated.
It remains impossible to confirm with certainty if this species was larger than Tyrannosaurus, which was long thought to be the biggest theropod.
The dimensions of Giganotosaurus fuel intense scientific discussion regarding the upper limits of size for theropod dinosaurs.
Some research places its existence between 113.2 and 106.3 million years ago during the Albian stage.
